client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really empty. Ever since my brother passed away last year, it’s like nothing brings me joy anymore. I try to hang out with friends, but I just feel disconnected, like they don’t really get what I’m going through. Honestly, I’m not sure if therapy can even help with something this heavy.
therapist:
I hear how deeply you're grieving your brother's loss and how this emptiness makes even familiar joys feel distant right now. That sense of isolation when others don't fully understand your pain must feel incredibly heavy to carry alone. 

Would it feel right to explore together what "help" might look like for you in this grieving process? There's no timeline for this kind of loss.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I don't even know what "help" would look like. Some days I think I should just power through it, but then I feel guilty for not grieving "correctly." And when people tell me it'll get better with time, that just makes me angry - like they're dismissing how permanent this loss feels.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of pressure about "how" to grieve, mixed with frustration when others try to comfort you in ways that don't land right. That anger when people suggest time will heal makes perfect sense - it can feel like they're minimizing the depth of your loss.

Would it help to talk about what feels most real and honest to you in this grieving process, without worrying about "correct" ways to do it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I guess what feels most real is just missing him every single day. Sometimes I want to talk about him, but I worry I'll bring people down or they'll think I'm stuck in the past. Other times I try to push through and act "normal," but that feels fake too. I don't know which way is right.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between honoring your grief and worrying about how others might perceive it. That tension between wanting to share memories and feeling like you need to "act normal" must be exhausting to navigate. 

What would it feel like to give yourself permission to miss him openly, without worrying about bringing others down? Your connection to him is precious, and your way of grieving is valid.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I could try letting myself miss him more openly, but I don't even know how to start. When I think about talking about him, I get overwhelmed - like I might break down completely. And I worry that if I let myself feel everything, I'll never be able to function normally again.
therapist:
It sounds like there's a lot of fear about what might happen if you truly let yourself feel the depth of your loss - like the grief might overwhelm you completely. That worry about not being able to function is completely understandable when you're facing such profound emotions. 

Perhaps we could start small - what's one memory of your brother that feels tender but manageable to share right now? Even just talking about him here could be a gentle first step.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I remember how he used to make these terrible puns that would make me groan, but secretly I loved them because they were so uniquely him. Sometimes I think about those moments and smile, but then I feel guilty for smiling, like I’m forgetting how much it hurts that he’s gone. It’s confusing - I don’t know if I should let myself feel the good memories or just focus on the pain.
therapist:
How beautiful that you can still feel his essence in those playful puns - it sounds like those memories carry both joy and sorrow in a way that feels tangled but precious. That guilt you feel when smiling shows how deeply you love him, not that you're forgetting the pain. 

Would it help to think that honoring the happy memories can be another way of keeping him close, rather than something that takes away from your grief? Both the smiles and the tears are part of loving him.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually makes a lot of sense... but sometimes when I think about the happy memories, it just makes the present feel even more empty by comparison. Like, remembering how he made me laugh just reminds me I'll never hear his laugh again. Is it normal for memories to feel comforting and painful at the same time?
therapist:
It's completely understandable that memories can feel both comforting and painful - that bittersweet mix shows how deeply you loved him. It's okay to let those feelings coexist; the love you shared wasn't simple, so it makes sense that remembering him wouldn't be either. 

Would it help to think of those memories as a way he continues to be part of your life, even if the laughter looks different now? The emptiness you feel shows how full your connection was.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I like the idea of seeing memories as a way he’s still part of my life... but honestly, sometimes it feels like holding onto those memories just makes the pain sharper. I worry that if I let myself think about him too much, I’ll never be able to move forward. How do I balance remembering him with continuing my own life?
therapist:
It sounds like you're wrestling with how to honor your brother's memory while also allowing yourself to grow and change - that's such a natural yet challenging part of grief. The way you're thinking deeply about this balance shows how much you care about both preserving his legacy and moving forward in a way that feels right for you. 

Perhaps we could explore what "moving forward" might look like for you - not forgetting him, but finding ways to carry him with you as you continue to live? There's no one right way to do this.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess moving forward would mean not crying every time I think of him, but that feels impossible right now. And part of me doesn't even want to stop crying - like if the pain fades, I'm losing my connection to him all over again. Is that selfish?
therapist:
Your voice carries such deep care in this worry - it's not selfish at all to fear that easing pain might mean losing your connection to him. That reluctance to let go of the tears shows how profoundly you love him. 

The way you're describing this makes me wonder - might there be ways to honor your bond that don't rely solely on the pain? Your connection was built on so much more than grief.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I never thought about it that way... that our connection wasn't just about the pain. But I guess that's true - we shared so many laughs and inside jokes and quiet moments too. It's just hard to focus on those when the loss feels so huge. I worry that if I try to remember the good times without the sadness, I'm somehow dishonoring his memory.
therapist:
It's clear how much you want to honor your brother's memory in a way that feels right to you. That fear of dishonoring him by remembering the joyful moments shows how deeply you care about preserving what you shared. 

Perhaps we could explore together how honoring him could include both the laughter and the tears? Your relationship was full of so many rich layers - it's okay to let them all coexist as part of how you keep him close.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I understand what you're saying, but it still feels really complicated. Part of me wants to try embracing both the joy and the pain, but another part worries I'll get stuck in the sadness forever if I let myself feel it fully. How do I know when I'm honoring him versus just dwelling in the grief?
therapist:
It sounds like you're thoughtfully navigating this tension between wanting to fully honor your brother while also being mindful of your own wellbeing - that's such an important balance to consider. Your voice has a hopeful quality as you talk about embracing both the joy and pain, even while you're understandably cautious about getting stuck in grief. 

What if we viewed this as an ongoing process rather than an either/or choice? Perhaps some days will feel more like honoring him, and others might feel more like dwelling - and that's okay. Would it help to explore what might make the difference between the two for you personally?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
